query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating an optimized volume fraction of tungsten carbide (WC) particles into a high‐entropy alloy (HEA) matrix will reduce both the coefficient of friction and wear rate by promoting in situ formation of hard carbide dispersions and lubricious oxide tribo‐films across a broad service‐temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A self‐lubricating HEA with a single-phase solid‐solution matrix that in its untreated state exhibits higher friction coefficients and relatively higher wear rates under sliding conditions.
generation.intervention: Integrate an optimized concentration (near 20–30 wt%) of WC particles into the HEA during synthesis/sintering (e.g., via spark plasma sintering or laser cladding) to form a composite.
generation.conditions: The intervention is expected to remain effective across a wide temperature range (from room temperature up to ~800 °C) and under sliding wear conditions typical for moving, self-lubricating components.
generation.structural_mediator: The presence of finely and uniformly dispersed WC particles, along with secondary carbide phases (e.g., Cr7C3, Co3W3C) that form at the interfaces between WC and the HEA matrix.
generation.mechanism: The WC additions increase the hardness and load-bearing capacity of the composite, reducing plastic deformation. Under frictional heating, the dispersed carbides induce formation of a protective, lubricious tribo-oxide film that mitigates abrasive and adhesive wear. This dual action (reinforcement by hard phases and self-generated lubrication) decreases both the friction coefficient and wear rate relative to the untreated HEA.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated HEA, the WC–HEA composite is expected to exhibit lower friction coefficients and significantly reduced wear rates under sliding conditions, while maintaining structural integrity over a wide temperature range.
generation.baseline: Untreated HEA material without added WC particles, which exhibits a higher friction coefficient and wear rate in comparative tribological tests.
generation.boundary: Exceeding the optimal WC content (e.g., >30 wt%) may lead to excessive formation of brittle phases and interface problems that could undermine bonding and negate the lubrication effect. The effect is also contingent on the proper processing to ensure uniform dispersion of WC particles.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimal WC loading and processing parameters may vary with the specific HEA composition and processing route. The temperature-dependent stability of the lubricious oxide film needs further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the base HEA without WC additions and one set of WC–HEA composites with an optimized WC content (~20–30 wt%). Subject both sets to standardized sliding wear tests (e.g., ball-on-disk) under controlled loads and at various temperatures spanning from room temperature to 800 °C. Ensure that all other processing parameters are held constant. Measure the friction coefficient continuously during the sliding tests and evaluate the wear rates via profilometry and microscopic imaging of the worn tracks.
measurements: Coefficient of friction over time at set temperatures
Wear volume loss from worn surface profilometry
Microstructural analysis (SEM/EDS) of tribo-film formation on worn surfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the WC–HEA composite does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the untreated HEA across the temperature range, or if the microstructural analysis reveals the absence of a stable, protective tribo-film associated with the intervention, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3. The Effect of WC Content on Properties of Composites
cited_evidence.text: WC particles have high hardness, good wear resistance, strong resistance to deformation during friction, and are less prone to plastic deformation, resulting in increased friction resistance and stronger wear resistance of the composites. With the increase of WC content, the wear mechanism of HEA matrix composites changes from adhesive wear to abrasive wear, and the formation of second phases such as Cr-rich and Co3W3C carbides in the composites also reduces the wear volume, which is beneficial to the improvement of wear resistance of HEA matrix. When the WC content increases to 30%, the WC content is too much, resulting in an excessive amount of the Cr-rich phase being generated in the composite, leading to more prominent interface problems, affecting the bonding between the hard phase and the matrix, resulting in a poor overall lubrication effect and increased friction coefficient of the composite. However, overall, compared with the Cr-rich phase, the distribution of WC particles in the 30 WC–HEA sample is more dispersed, and the effect of WC is more prominent. In this work, WC-FeCoCrNi composites were prepared by the SPS process. The effects of WC content on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and wear resistance of WC–HEA composites were studied. The main conclusions are as follows: A single-phase FCC solid solution structure was formed after SPS sintering of the HEA pure matrix powder, which did not appear before sintering, indicating that SPS is helpful for HEA to complete alloying. The sintered WC–HEA composite is mainly composed of an FCC matrix phase (Ni, Fe) and carbide phases (Cr7C3, Co3W3C, WC, etc.). With the increase of WC content, the distribution of WC is dispersed, and the content of Cr7C3 and Co3W3C increases gradually. Some needle-like Cr-rich phases in the FCC matrix coarsen into flakes. Although the addition of WC reduces the densification of the composite to a certain extent, it significantly improves the hardness and compressive yield strength of the matrix. The microhardness of the 30 WC–HEA composite is the highest, at 459.2 HV, which is 71.2% higher than that of the pure matrix material.
